overview: “Eastern North American hunter-gatherers” is the atlas’s catch-all for 500 to 1492, not an ancient name or a single people. At 500 its fourteen pieces wrap around separately mapped Hopewell, Swift Creek, Marksville and Point Peninsula. At 600 the software expands it into two enormous components from Atlantic Canada to Florida and the upper Mississippi. Real life was less tidy. Communities spoke different languages, moved and traded, built camps, villages, towns and cities, and combined fishing, hunting, gathering, gardens and intensive maize farming. Cahokia grew into a major urban center; Moundville, Etowah, Aztalan and Werowocomoco followed their own histories. Archaeologists recover postholes, hearths, seeds, bones, teeth, residues, middens, mounds, pottery, isotope signatures and altered landscapes, then test interpretations against dates and living Indigenous knowledge. Evidence from one place never becomes a continent-wide rule. In 1492 the atlas swaps the umbrella for many named Indigenous homelands and a few gaps. No population suddenly acquired those names or vanished at that seam. Nations, families, languages, farms, fisheries, ceremonies and political communities continued into the violent, uneven era of European invasion.

periods.title: 500 to 600: fourteen atlas pieces surround named archaeological regions
periods.summary: The first target geometry is a fourteen-component patchwork beside separately colored Hopewell, Swift Creek, Marksville, Point Peninsula, Laurel, Copena, Porter and other labels. Local Woodland communities combined horticulture, hunting, exchange and settlement in varied ways; the blanketing name cannot turn those neighbors into fixed ethnic borders.

periods.title: 600 to 700: the umbrella expands while effigy traditions remain regional
periods.summary: At 600 the atlas absorbs many earlier cutouts and becomes a two-component envelope, an editorial consolidation rather than a mass migration. Along the upper Mississippi, people built animal-shaped and other mounds, lived in nearby villages, used wetlands, hunted and fished, gathered plants, and tended gardens within a specifically regional history.

periods.title: 700 to 800: copied borders conceal sharply different food systems
periods.summary: The 700 map copies the 600 target coordinates exactly. Upper Mississippi evidence instead shows regional divergence: some communities intensified horticulture while maize remained climatically limited farther north. Pottery, fishing, wild rice, gardens and settlement schedules varied, so an unchanged polygon cannot mean a century of social or ecological sameness.

periods.title: 800 to 900: towns and fields grow beyond a one-word economy
periods.summary: A one-position coordinate revision leaves all audited sample places unchanged. At Aztalan, residents enclosed a twenty-one-acre town, built houses with central hearths and raised platform mounds while cultivating fields beyond the wall. Such farming and planned settlement expose “hunter-gatherers” as a particularly poor description of many people inside the map color.

periods.title: 900 to 1000: Mississippian developments appear through local histories
periods.summary: The target changes by only two positions, but central Georgia saw a new Macon Plateau settlement tradition around 900. Residents farmed, stored surplus, hunted, made pottery and textiles, built staged mounds and gathered in an earth lodge. That Ocmulgee history is one regional transformation, not the birth of one eastern civilization.

periods.title: 1000 to 1100: Cahokia grows while the atlas line barely twitches
periods.summary: Tiny coordinate differences leave sampled membership stable. Cahokia expanded dramatically around 1050 into the largest known precontact city north of Mexico, with mounds, a grand plaza, neighborhoods, a stockade and aligned post circles. Its scale matters, but the same umbrella also covers small farms, fishing camps and unrelated northern communities.

periods.title: 1100 to 1200: cups preserve evidence for a far-traveled drink
periods.summary: The atlas returns to its 900 geometry while local networks keep changing. Chemical analysis of Cahokian beakers dated 1050 to 1250 found caffeine, theobromine and ursolic acid consistent with Ilex drinks. Holly grew far south, so a special beverage reveals exchange and ritual without proving that everyone drank it or shared one religion.

periods.title: 1200 to 1279: Moundville reorganizes a river valley landscape
periods.summary: The 1200 map again reuses the broad 900 envelope. Moundville’s palisaded town, plaza and earthen platforms developed within a densely settled Black Warrior Valley, and its political and residential roles changed over time. A shared archaeological pattern links many places, but “Mississippian” remains a modern scholarly category rather than a self-name.

periods.title: 1279 to 1300: a software seam meets changing households and clans
periods.summary: The atlas inserts a twenty-one-year interval with minute coordinate rounding and no sampled ownership change. Descendant-informed Moundville interpretation describes maize towns, mound labor, matrilineal clans and unequal authority, while stressing that many distinct communities are grouped under the Mississippian label. Those social details cannot be extended automatically across the entire polygon.

periods.title: 1300 to 1400: the line freezes while centers decentralize
periods.summary: The 1300 target geometry exactly repeats 1279. Local histories do not freeze: Moundville’s residential population declined as ceremonial use continued, while other towns grew, shifted or dispersed. Archaeological phases and political centers end at different times, so no evidence supports one synchronized eastern collapse hidden beneath the copied border.

periods.title: 1400 to 1492: thriving villages approach an atlas category swap
periods.summary: The final target has tiny coordinate changes but stable audited membership. At mid-fifteenth-century Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha, St Lawrence Iroquoians occupied a large village with houses, middens, pottery, bone tools, maize, beans, squash, sunflower and wild foods. At 1492 the umbrella disappears; it does not take such communities with it.

sections.title: Begin with the atlas, then dismantle its giant label

items.text: The index contains one exact later record dated approximately 500 to 1492, with eleven continuous border intervals and no prior card or override. A different exact id already has a card for 1500 to 100 BCE. Six centuries of atlas silence and radically different evidence make a separate later card the honest choice.

At 500 the target is a fourteen-component patchwork with many named archaeological cutouts. By 600 it becomes two huge components, and later files make only tiny coordinate changes. Shared topology arcs meet subarctic, plains and Caloosahatchee labels. These are software tiling facts, not ancient treaties, borders or ethnic membership tests.

The phrase “hunter-gatherers” badly understates this thousand-year interval. Some communities relied heavily on fishing, hunting and wild plants; others tended native crops or farmed maize intensively; many combined them. Camps, hamlets, dispersed farms, palisaded villages and cities all occur. One subsistence label cannot carry that much historical luggage without dropping several suitcases.

Evidence comes from settlement plans, postholes, hearths, storage and refuse pits, plant and animal remains, pottery, residues, mounds, burials, teeth, isotope ratios and lake sediments. Each answers different questions. A corn cob can show maize use; it cannot identify the grower’s language, clan, favorite recipe or opinion of the neighbor’s cooking.

Written-language sample for 500 to 1492: none is securely attributable to this whole umbrella. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. Spiro iconography and Mi’kmaw rock images are meaningful visual systems, but dates and linguistic readings do not supply one transcribable eastern language sample. Borrowing a later alphabet would invent false unity.

sections.title: Watch Late Woodland communities choose different paths

items.text: At Ocmulgee, Woodland communities used horticulture to support more settled life, produced tools and art, and participated in wide exchange. This local account corrects the idea that everyone simply followed game. It also stops short of claiming permanent towns, the same crops or identical leaders across every forest, coast and river valley.

Upper Mississippi effigy mounds took forms such as birds, bears and water spirits between about 650 and 1200. Nearby villages used wetlands, hunted, fished, gathered wild foods and grew sunflower and squash. The earthworks may have marked ceremony, burial or territory; archaeologists do not possess a single ancient instruction manual for every mound.

Late Woodland economies varied even along one river. In southeastern Minnesota, corn and beans grew more important, while farther north climate constrained maize and other foods remained central. Pottery styles and settlements also differed. “Eastern” is a direction on the map, not a recipe that everyone cooked on the same schedule.

Crystal River’s estuary supported a long-lived, sedentary Florida population and ceremonial center. People adopted outside ideas and technologies while retaining local identity. Coastal abundance, mound building and visiting traders do not turn its residents into miniature Cahokians, nor do they prove that an inland family in Ohio ate or worshiped similarly.

At Maryland’s Harrison site, dated Late Woodland deposits include a possible shelter around 1060 and a shell midden around 1170. Residues indicate hunting, butchering, plant and fish processing, and hide work. That combination shows mobile or seasonal activity persisted beside village farming elsewhere; “settled” and “mobile” were choices, not evolutionary grades.

sections.title: Eat from farms, forests, rivers, marshes and very busy pots

items.text: Eastern food systems never became maize monocultures everywhere. New synthesis shows that older native crops and managed forests continued even at Cahokia and into colonial disruption. Sunflower, squash, chenopod and other plants could grow beside maize, while nuts, fruits, game and aquatic foods buffered risk and kept meals regionally distinct.

Charred maize at the Shepard site gives direct evidence of Late Woodland farming beside a Potomac village midden containing mussel shell, animal bone, pottery and stone tools. Each remain entered the deposit differently, so archaeologists reconstruct meals by combining contexts. One heroic burnt kernel cannot narrate the entire dinner by itself.

Around northeast Florida in 1000, salt marshes supplied fish, crustaceans and oysters. People built branch-and-vine weirs that trapped animals as tides fell, a clever technology demanding repeated repair and ecological knowledge. The reconstruction also describes specialist crafts and council houses, but it belongs to this coastal setting, not every atlas component.

Emerald Mound’s builders were skillful farmers of corn, beans and squash who also ate game, fish, roots, nuts and berries. Large populations depended on this mixed system. Farming increased storage and planning needs; it did not abolish hunting or gathering, and the crop trio should never erase hundreds of locally important foods.

Cahokian beakers kept molecular traces of an Ilex drink even after leaves and liquid vanished. Holly had to travel hundreds of kilometers north, making each caffeinated serving a small map of exchange. Fun fact: special-event caffeine is at least nine centuries older than the office coffee machine, although its ceremonies were entirely different.

sections.title: Build cities, towns, villages and political worlds

items.text: Cahokia covered about four thousand acres and may have held ten to twenty thousand people at its peak around 1100. Residents raised more than a hundred mounds, planned a grand plaza, built neighborhoods, stockades and aligned post circles. The city proves monumental urbanism; it does not prove political control over the atlas’s Atlantic coastline.

Strontium in teeth shows that about one-third of sampled Cahokians were nonlocal and came from multiple geological regions. Many moved during late childhood or adolescence. The city grew through migration as well as local families, making it socially diverse. Isotopes reveal childhood landscapes, not personal names, spoken languages or motives for moving.

Moundville was a three-hundred-acre palisaded town with a central plaza and twenty-six mounds. Its heaviest residential phase later shifted toward ceremonial and political use. Archaeologists still debate both its rise and decline. A city can change function without its people evaporating, and an abandoned house is not an abandoned ancestry.

Etowah joined six mounds, a plaza, village, borrow pits and a defensive ditch beside a river. Residents farmed, hunted, fished, traded and produced accomplished art. Differences in burial and mound-top buildings show unequal status, but one priest-chief model cannot be pasted automatically onto every Mississippian town or smaller farming community.

Werowocomoco began developing around 1200 as a Chesapeake town where people built homes, planted crops and raised families. Archaeology identifies politics, ceremony and trade long before English accounts made Powhatan famous. Tribal collaboration now guides stewardship, helping the site tell Indigenous history without making a colonist’s arrival the opening chapter.

sections.title: Shape copper, shell, clay, wood and whole landscapes

items.text: Aztalan residents set posts, plastered walls with clay and grass, roofed houses with thatch and kept central hearths. Outside the enclosure they cultivated corn, squash, beans and other crops. Building a twenty-one-acre walled settlement demanded surveying, forestry, earthwork and maintenance; the wall may have separated spaces as well as defended them.

Mississippian metalsmiths hammered native copper into thin sheets, raised designs, riveted pieces and embellished surfaces with symbolic motifs. Conservation imaging reveals tool marks and fabrication choices invisible at a glance. Copper-working was skilled transformation without smelting; “soft metal” certainly did not mean “easy art project,” especially after hours of careful hammering.

At Raleigh Island, LiDAR and excavation reveal a shell-ring complex where people made large quantities of shell beads around 900 to 1200. Production linked Gulf materials to wider Mississippian exchange. A workshop demonstrates specialized knowledge and labor, but finished beads alone cannot identify every maker, trading partner or meaning attached to wearing them.

Russell Cave interpretation highlights shell-tempered clay vessels formed by coiling, smoothing and firing. Crushed shell improved performance, while bowls and plates suited changing meals. Pottery recipes carried learned choices, and distant ornaments show exchange. Similar vessels can mark interaction without proving that potters shared one language, lineage or political boss.

Spiro linked an elite village and mound center to far-reaching political, religious and economic networks. Carved shell, copper, textiles and imagery preserve extraordinary visual knowledge. The Oklahoma Historical Society calls some of it an iconographic writing system, but scholars cannot transliterate it into one securely identified spoken language for this atlas umbrella.

sections.title: Live in households, extended families and unequal communities

items.text: Domestic architecture and pottery at early Moundville reveal clusters of several households rather than isolated nuclear families. Kin-like groups hosted feasts, shared risk and practiced household ceremony, while non-elites retained meaningful autonomy. Archaeology can map repeated activities and buildings more confidently than it can assign every resident a precise family relationship.

At Southwold, several hundred people lived in longhouses housing extended families related through a common maternal ancestor. Double palisades enclosed the fifteenth-century village. This is unusually clear evidence for one Iroquoian community near the window’s end; it is not a warrant to label every eastern household matrilineal or every dwelling a longhouse.

Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha preserves twenty-five structures, two middens, pottery, pipes, bone tools, ornaments, cooking bones and thousands of plant remains. Those deposits reveal meals and shared spaces in a large village. They do not give a household census: grandparents, adoptees, visitors and neighbors can all leave traces around the same structure.

Late Haudenosaunee longhouses contained several family compartments and shared hearths, with bark platforms, suspended storage and tall maize bins. Smoke rose above sleeping level and fleas apparently ignored family boundaries. Museum evidence is closest to the window’s end, so it illuminates one tradition rather than supplying a timeless eastern floor plan.

Descendant-informed Moundville interpretation describes matrilineal clans and leadership transmitted through a mother’s family. That makes women central to political continuity as well as farming and household life. The evidence belongs to Moundville and connected southeastern traditions; social rules elsewhere could differ, and “women’s work” should not become an automatic artifact label.

sections.title: Grow up by watching, practicing, traveling and playing

items.text: Fingernail impressions on fifteenth-century Ontario pottery let researchers test whether children handled clay and learned vessel making. Prints are rare, delicate evidence: nail size can suggest small hands but cannot identify a child’s name, teacher or skill level. Still, the pots literally preserve young people touching the material record.

Cahokia’s isotope study suggests many nonlocal people arrived in late childhood or adolescence. Young movers learned new routes, foods, manners and alliances while carrying knowledge from earlier homes. Teeth record geological differences during formation, not whether a move was chosen, joyful, coerced, family-led or accompanied by a spectacularly bored teenager.

Ocmulgee evidence and later comparison describe chunkey, in which players aimed spears near a rolling stone disk, and a team ball game used between towns. Games trained bodies, drew spectators and carried social meaning. Archaeology preserves disks better than trash talk, referees or the exact moment someone insisted the stone took a bad bounce.

Making a durable shell-tempered pot required finding clay and temper, preparing both, controlling coil thickness, smoothing walls and managing fire. Russell Cave’s artifacts preserve results rather than lessons. Children and novices must have practiced many skills somewhere, but no reviewed source gives a standard apprenticeship age, school calendar or universal teaching method.

A Droulers child could have watched planting, cooking, fishing, tool making and house repair in a village full of repeated work. Learning likely happened through participation, storytelling, correction and practice. That is a reasoned inference from material complexity, not proof of identical parenting, childhood stages or classroom-like instruction across Iroquoian communities.

sections.title: Read health in bones and teeth without inventing a clinic

items.text: Bones and teeth can record anemia-related changes, infection, joint wear, trauma and diet, but most skeletal responses are nonspecific. Many short illnesses leave no trace, and excavated people are not a perfect population sample. Paleopathology can reveal patterns; it cannot diagnose every fever, headache, birth complication or treatment that once mattered.

Some Illinois Mississippian samples show more infection and iron-related stress as dense settlement and maize dependence increased, with serious effects among children and women. Agriculture fed larger communities but could narrow diets and spread illness. These patterns are local and statistical, not a verdict that farming made every person sicker everywhere.

Late Cahokian isotope and dental research identifies subpopulations with different diets and health experiences. A city was not one biological average: neighborhood, origin, status, work and food access mattered. Even strong chemical evidence reconstructs consumed foods more readily than affection, nursing care, grief or the practical knowledge used during recovery.

Comparisons of Mississippian elites and non-elites find no single neat pattern. Some high-status people ate more animal protein, while trauma, disease and nutrition varied among sites and groups. Fancy burial goods therefore do not equal perfect health, and a simple skeleton ranking cannot substitute for the complicated lives behind political inequality.

Etowah interpretation notes trees used for food and medicine, and Effigy Mounds education mentions locally gathered medicinal herbs. Plants could also serve ritual, flavor, fiber or fuel, so this card will not invent a universal prescription list. Healers and caregivers existed, but no shared eastern clinic, dosage chart or medical school survives.

sections.title: Fetch water, sweep refuse and investigate the toilet question

items.text: Cahokia’s wet ridge-and-swale floodplain shaped mound placement, neighborhoods, causeways and plazas. Water carried people, food and meaning, but also brought mud, insects and flood risk. Archaeologists can map natural and built water features; the reviewed study does not reveal equal access, a pipe network or what every household considered clean.

At the Winslow village, semi-circular refuse pits held ash, charcoal, broken pots, animal bone, shell, fire-cracked rock and stone-working debris. Their arrangement helps reconstruct household and community space. A refuse pit shows organized disposal after use, though contents may accumulate, be moved or mix; it is not automatically a toilet.

Harrison’s shell midden and processing residues show food waste accumulating near a repeatedly used Chesapeake place. Shells preserve dramatically, while wood, fiber, odors and many organic remains disappear. The archaeological garbage pile is therefore a biased roommate: wonderfully informative about some meals and almost silent about yesterday’s sweeping routine.

A recent Angel Mounds study found chemical and microscopic features consistent with human excreta placed in one abandoned fourteenth-century house basin. The authors treat this as secondary disposal and a new sanitation question. It is valuable direct evidence, but one reused basin is not a citywide latrine design or sewer system.

Toilet report: no standard facility is securely documented for the whole atlas category. Winslow pits handled refuse, and Angel may preserve deliberate excreta disposal after a house was abandoned. People managed waste somehow, but privacy, cleaning, water protection and location rules remain local questions. Ancient poop finally spoke; it gave one address, not zoning law.

sections.title: Face power, conflict, climate change and an ending that is not extinction

items.text: Horseshoe Lake chemistry indicates persistent drying from roughly 1200 to 1400 during Cahokia’s decentralization. Drought could strain crops, authority and migration decisions, but the researchers do not make climate a single automatic cause. Political tension, violence, environmental change and household choices interacted, and other regions inside the polygon followed different paths.

Another lake-core study finds that Cahokia arose during centuries with fewer major Mississippi floods and declined after large floods returned. Floodplain farming offered rich soil and serious risk. This correlation strengthens an environmental explanation without making a flood press a civilization’s off switch; people adapted, relocated and reorganized over generations.

Fecal stanols in Horseshoe Lake indicate the Cahokia region reached a population low around 1400 and grew again by about 1500. That invisible chemical signal challenges the old “lost civilization” story. A famous center declined, but Indigenous people returned, moved through and lived in the watershed beyond its monumental peak.

Winterville’s mounds were enlarged by countless basket loads carried and tamped by community members. Archaeological and historical evidence links the site with ancestors of the Natchez. Continuity is specific and carefully investigated, not a license to match every ancient mound to one modern nation, yet it firmly rejects the fantasy of ownerless ruins.

At 1492 the atlas replaces one color with many overlapping homeland labels, including Mi’kmaw, Wampanoag, Lenape, Haudenosaunee, Shawnee, Muscogee, Chickasaw, Natchez and others. The redraw is imperfect and not a birth certificate. Living Tribal Nations still guide Moundville interpretation and repatriation, so the proper ending is continuity, sovereignty and many histories.

ending.text: At 1492 the atlas deletes its enormous “Eastern North American hunter-gatherers” layer and draws many named, overlapping Indigenous homelands, while leaving some places blank. That is a software legend change, not a shared fall, conquest or migration. The communities beneath the old color already had their own names, languages, alliances, towns, farms, fisheries, hunting territories, ceremonies and family histories. European invasion and epidemic disease reached different regions later and unevenly; they must not be used to make Indigenous life disappear at a round map date. Archaeological sites also continued along different paths: Cahokia had decentralized, Moundville changed roles, and towns such as Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha and Werowocomoco flourished. Living Tribal Nations remain historical actors and partners in interpretation, protection and repatriation. The override therefore keeps fell null, names no automatic successor, and records plural continuity beyond an editorial endpoint.
